ai.definition: Carbon-negative cement is a type of cement that not only reduces CO2 emissions compared to traditional cement but also actively absorbs CO2 throughout its lifecycle, effectively becoming a net absorber of carbon dioxide.
ai.howItWorks: The process involves enhancing the mineral carbonation properties of cement by using specific additives or minerals during production. These materials react with atmospheric CO2 during curing, locking it into the concrete matrix, thereby increasing the overall carbon sequestration capacity of the cement product.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the significant greenhouse gas emissions from the construction industry, which is a major contributor to global CO2 levels.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves adding minerals or additives that promote mineral carbonation during the production of cement. This can be done through modifications in raw material selection and processing techniques.
ai.buildProcess: During construction, carbon-negative cement behaves similarly to conventional cement but with enhanced carbon sequestration properties. It is typically used in concrete mixtures for building structures like roads, bridges, and buildings.
ai.costDrivers: Higher initial production costs due to the need for specialized additives or minerals, as well as potential energy-intensive manufacturing processes required to incorporate these materials effectively.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to gain traction in infrastructure projects where carbon sequestration benefits can be demonstrated and valued.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations targeting carbon-negative cement. However, it may benefit from existing green building codes and initiatives that encourage the use of low-carbon materials.
ai.risks: Technical challenges in scaling up production while maintaining cost-effectiveness and performance; potential regulatory barriers if standards for carbon sequestration are not yet established.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to current market conditions, but it could become more viable as demand for low-carbon materials increases.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development may focus on improving the efficiency of CO2 absorption and reducing production costs through optimized manufacturing processes and new additive technologies.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking, which can consume significant electricity depending on scale.

glossary.def: A process where minerals react with CO2 to form stable carbonate compounds, effectively sequestering the carbon dioxide.
The capture and long-term storage of atmospheric CO2 to mitigate climate change impacts.

subsystems.name: Binder feedstock
subsystems.role: supplies calcium without the CO2 that limestone releases when it is burned.
parts: calcium silicate or magnesium silicate rock
steel slag and cement kiln dust
calcined clay or slag as supplementary cementitious material

subsystems.name: CO2 supply
subsystems.role: provides the gas that will be locked into the material.
parts: capture unit on an industrial flue

subsystems.name: Batching and mixing
subsystems.role: mixes the binder, aggregate and water; in one route, CO2 is injected here.

subsystems.name: Carbonation curing
subsystems.role: reacts CO2 with calcium compounds to form calcite, which fills pores, gives early strength and stores carbon.

subsystems.name: Reinforcement and structural design
subsystems.role: keeps the element safe where steel rebar is needed.
parts: rebar, or non-corroding fibre and stainless alternatives

subsystems.name: Verification and accounting
subsystems.role: proves how much CO2 was absorbed, not just claimed.
parts: thermogravimetric and XRD analysis of samples

buildSteps.title: Choose the calcium source
buildSteps.detail: Instead of limestone, which releases CO2 when burned, the route uses calcium silicate rock, steel slag, demolition fines or other waste calcium — or avoids high-temperature clinker altogether.

buildSteps.title: Capture the CO2
buildSteps.detail: Concentrated CO2 is captured from a cement kiln, power plant or the air, then dried, compressed and stored for use.

buildSteps.title: Batch the mix
buildSteps.detail: Binder, sand, aggregate and water are weighed and mixed; in the injection route, CO2 is dosed into the fresh mix, where it forms nanoscale calcium carbonate particles that help the concrete flow and gain strength.

buildSteps.title: Cast the element
buildSteps.detail: The mix is poured into moulds for blocks, pavers, pipes, wall panels or other precast products — shapes that fit inside a sealed curing chamber.

buildSteps.title: Cure under CO2
buildSteps.detail: The element sits in a chamber with a controlled CO2-rich atmosphere, humidity and temperature for hours; the gas reacts with calcium silicates and hydroxide to form calcite and a silica gel that binds the mix together.

buildSteps.title: Test and tune
buildSteps.detail: Samples are crushed for strength and analysed to measure how much CO2 was actually mineralised, typically a few percent of the binder mass, and the recipe is adjusted.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and monitor
buildSteps.detail: Products go into buildings, roads and drainage works; the concrete continues to absorb small amounts of CO2 from the air over decades as carbonation slowly moves inward.

buildSteps.title: Prove the net result
buildSteps.detail: A full life-cycle assessment adds up process emissions, energy, transport, and both the stored and reabsorbed CO2 to check the product really is below zero.

prerequisites.why: carbonation needs a concentrated gas stream, and capture is still the costliest part of the chain.
quarrying and grinding silicate rock at scale is proven in mining but not yet as a cement feed.
kilns, grinders and electrochemical reactors must run on clean power or the carbon maths fails.
carbonation drops the concrete's pH, so ordinary rebar can rust unless design or materials change.

prerequisites.tech: Standards and certification for negative emissions
prerequisites.why: building codes and carbon-accounting rules do not yet reliably recognise stored CO2 in concrete.

pathway.milestone: CO2 injection and carbonation curing in precast plants, cutting cement content and storing CO2 in blocks, pavers and pipes
pathway.unlocks: a commercial, verifiable way to put carbon into building products.

pathway.milestone: blended low-clinker binders combined with carbonation curing
pathway.unlocks: precast products approaching or crossing net zero.

pathway.milestone: demonstration cement made from calcium silicate rock or by electrochemical routes that release no process CO2
pathway.unlocks: a binder whose production is near-zero before any carbonation credit.

pathway.milestone: net-negative structural ready-mix concrete with certified accounting
pathway.unlocks: large infrastructure acting as a durable carbon store.
